Existence of global weak solutions
to a Cahn–Hilliard cross-diffusion system
in lymphangiogenesisThanks: The authors acknowledge partial support from the Austrian Science Fund (FWF), grants P33010 and F65. This work has received funding from the European Research Council (ERC) under the European Union’s Horizon 2020 research and innovation programme, ERC Advanced Grant no. 101018153.

Ansgar Jüngel Address: Institute of Analysis and Scientific Computing, Technische Universität, Wiedner Hauptstraße 8–10, 1040 Wien, Austria Email address: juengel@tuwien.ac.at and Yue Li Address: Institute of Analysis and Scientific Computing, Technische Universität, Wiedner Hauptstraße 8-10, 1040 Wien, Austria Email address: yue.li@asc.tuwien.ac.at
Date: August 24, 2026
Abstract.

The global-in-time existence of weak solutions to a degenerate Cahn–Hilliard cross-diffusion system with singular potential in a bounded domain with no-flux boundary conditions is proved. The model consists of two coupled parabolic fourth-order partial differential equations and describes the evolution of the fiber phase volume fraction and the solute concentration, modeling the pre-patterning of lymphatic vessel morphology. The fiber phase fraction satisfies the segregation property if this holds initially. The existence proof is based on a three-level approximation scheme and a priori estimates coming from the energy and entropy inequalities. While the free energy is nonincreasing in time, the entropy is only bounded because of the cross-diffusion coupling.

Key words and phrases: 
Cahn–Hilliard equation; cross-diffusion equations; degenerate mobility; singular potential; entropy; weak solutions.
2000 Mathematics Subject Classification
35D30, 35K35, 35K65, 35K67, 92C37.

1. Introduction

Lymphangiogenesis describes the formation of lymphatic vessels from pre-existing ones similar to angiogenesis. In this paper, we analyze a two-phase diffusion system modeling the pre-patterning of lymphatic vessel morphology in collagen gels. The model, first suggested in [21], describes the interaction of the collagen gel with a solute, such as protons and nutrients. The equations have been modified and given a thermodynamically consistent form in [17]. They describe the evolution of the volume fractions of the fiber phase ϕ⁡(x,t)\phi(x,t) and fluid phase 1−ϕ⁡(x,t)1-\phi(x,t) as well as the concentration c⁡(x,t)c(x,t) of the solute. The unknowns are solutions to the cross-diffusion equations

(1.1) ∂tϕ\displaystyle\partial_{t}\phi =div(M(ϕ)(∇μ−c∇∂cf(ϕ,c))),\displaystyle=\operatorname{div}\big(M(\phi)(\nabla\mu-c\nabla\partial_{c}f(\phi,c))\big),
(1.2) ∂tc\displaystyle\partial_{t}c =−div(cM(ϕ)(∇μ−c∇∂cf(ϕ,c)))+div(ce−ϕ∇∂cf(ϕ,c)),\displaystyle=-\operatorname{div}\big(cM(\phi)(\nabla\mu-c\nabla\partial_{c}f(\phi,c))\big)+\operatorname{div}\big(ce^{-\phi}\nabla\partial_{c}f(\phi,c)\big),
(1.3) μ\displaystyle\mu =−Δϕ+∂ϕf(ϕ,c)in Ω,t>0,\displaystyle=-\Delta\phi+\partial_{\phi}f(\phi,c)\quad\mbox{in }\Omega,\ t>0,

where Ω⊂ℝd\Omega\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{d} (d≥1d\geq 1) is a bounded domain and ∂c=∂/∂c\partial_{c}=\partial/\partial c, ∂ϕ=∂/∂ϕ\partial_{\phi}=\partial/\partial\phi are partial derivatives. The (degenerate) mobility is given as in [21] by

(1.4) M⁡(ϕ)=ϕ2​(1−ϕ)2,M(\phi)=\phi^{2}(1-\phi)^{2},

and the energy density reads as

(1.5) f⁡(ϕ,c)=ϕ​log⁡ϕ+(1−ϕ)​log⁡(1−ϕ)+ϕ⁡(1−ϕ)+c22+c⁡(1−ϕ).f(\phi,c)=\phi\log\phi+(1-\phi)\log(1-\phi)+\phi(1-\phi)+\frac{c^{2}}{2}+c(1-\phi).

The first three terms represent the (nonconvex) Flory–Huggins energy [10, 14], and the last two terms are the nutrient energy [13, (2.63)]. The potential ∂ϕf⁡(ϕ,c)\partial_{\phi}f(\phi,c) in (1.2) contains the term log⁡(ϕ/(1−ϕ))\log(\phi/(1-\phi)) which is singular at ϕ=0\phi=0 and ϕ=1\phi=1. The coefficient c​e−ϕce^{-\phi} can be interpreted as the effective diffusion of solute in the fluid phase [21, (4)]. Observe that the corresponding term is different from the diffusion in [21] because of thermodynamic considerations; see [17, Section 2] for details on the derivation of the model.

Equations (1.1)–(1.3) are supplemented by initial and no-flux boundary conditions,

(1.6) ϕ⁡(0)=ϕ0,c⁡(0)=c0\displaystyle\phi(0)=\phi_{0},\quad c(0)=c_{0} in ​Ω,\displaystyle\quad\mbox{in }\Omega,
(1.7) ∇ϕ⋅ν=c∇c⋅ν=cM(ϕ)∇μ⋅ν=0\displaystyle\nabla\phi\cdot\nu=c\nabla c\cdot\nu=cM(\phi)\nabla\mu\cdot\nu=0 on ​∂Ω,t>0.\displaystyle\quad\mbox{on }\partial\Omega,\ t>0.

Model (1.1)–(1.3) is a fourth-order cross-diffusion system with the following features. If the chemical potential μ\mu is constant, the diffusion matrix associated to the variables (ϕ,c)(\phi,c) has a vanishing eigenvalue. This indicates that it is more convenient to work with the thermodynamic variables (μ,∂cf)(\mu,\partial_{c}f) (see below). If the nutrient energy is constant, we obtain the Cahn–Hilliard equation for phase separation with a nonconvex energy. Our aim is to prove the global existence of weak solutions to (1.1)–(1.7).

1.1. State of the art

The study of two-phase models is stimulated by various applications modeling, for instance, tumor growth [6], biofilm growth [24], or formation of lymphatic vessels [21]. The mathematical modeling of lymphangiogenesis is rather recent. A discrete compartment model of the lymphatic system was already presented in the 1970s [19]. More recently, a differential equations model was presented in [1]. The work [11] analyzed a diffusion system with haptotaxis and chemotaxis terms for tumor lymphangiogenesis. The collagen pre-pattering caused by interstitial fluid flow is modeled in [21] by Cahn–Hilliard-type equations. It was found in [22] that a hexagonal lymphatic capillary network is optimal in terms of fluid drainage, confirmed by experiments in mouse tails and human skin. This hexagonal structure was also found in numerical simulations in two space dimensions [17].

The Cahn–Hilliard model was introduced in [3] to study phase separations in binary alloys. The first existence analysis of Cahn–Hilliard equations was given in [9] in one space dimension and in [8] in several space dimensions. The existence and uniqueness of solutions to the Cahn–Hilliard system strictly depend on the properties of the mobility M⁡(ϕ)M(\phi) (degenerate or nondegenerate) and the potential ∂ϕf⁡(ϕ,c)\partial_{\phi}f(\phi,c) (singular or regular). Since the Cahn–Hilliard equations do not admit a comparison principle, lower and upper bounds for the phase variable cannot generally be obtained. A sufficient condition for the property 0≤ϕ≤10\leq\phi\leq 1 (if satisfied initially) is a degenerate mobility M⁡(ϕ)M(\phi) [25] or a singular potential [2]. We refer to the book [18] for more details and references.

Diffusion systems with Cahn–Hilliard terms were analyzed more recently, in particular in the context of biological membranes [12] and tumor growth modeling [20]. In these models, the cross diffusion is of Keller–Segel type and thus, the diffusion matrix is triangular, which simplifies the analysis. In [15], Maxwell–Stefan models for fluid mixtures with full diffusion matrix and Cahn–Hilliard-type chemical potentials were investigated. Finally, a Cahn–Hilliard cross-diffusion model arising in thin-film solar cell fabrication was analyzed in [4, 7]. The techniques of these papers, however, cannot be employed for our model. In particular, the existence analysis of model (1.1)–(1.3) is new up to our knowledge.

1.3. Main result

We first define our notion of weak solution.

Definition 1.1 (Weak solution).

Let T>0T>0 be arbitrary and set ΩT:=(0,T)×Ω\Omega_{T}:=(0,T)\times\Omega. The function (ϕ,c)(\phi,c) is called a weak solution to problem (1.1)–(1.7) on [0,T][0,T] if (ϕ,c)(\phi,c) satisfies 0<ϕ<10<\phi<1, c≥0c\geq 0 in ΩT\Omega_{T},

Since it is difficult to derive an upper bound for cc, we cannot expect that the weak formulation of the equation for cc holds for ψ2∈L2​(0,T,H1​(Ω))\psi_{2}\in L^{2}(0,T;H^{1}(\Omega)). Because of the degeneracy, we cannot expect a gradient bound for μ\mu, but we obtain M⁡(ϕ)∇μ∈L2(0,T;L4/3(Ω))\sqrt{M(\phi)}\nabla\mu\in L^{2}(0,T;L^{4/3}(\Omega)).

Our existence result reads as follows.

Theorem 1.2.

Let Ω⊂ℝd\Omega\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{d} (d≤4)(d\leq 4) be a bounded domain with boundary ∂Ω∈C2\partial\Omega\in C^{2}, let T>0T>0, and let ϕ0∈H1​(Ω)\phi_{0}\in H^{1}(\Omega), c0∈L2​(Ω)c_{0}\in L^{2}(\Omega) satisfy 0<ϕ∗≤ϕ0≤1−ϕ∗<10<\phi_{*}\leq\phi_{0}\leq 1-\phi_{*}<1, c0≥0c_{0}\geq 0 in Ω\Omega for some ϕ∗∈(0,1)\phi_{*}\in(0,1). Then problem (1.1)–(1.7) possesses a weak solution (ϕ,c)(\phi,c) in [0,T][0,T] in the sense of Definition 1.1.

The proof is based on an approximation procedure. We introduce three approximation levels. First, we remove the degeneracy in M⁡(ϕ)M(\phi) and the singularities in f⁡(ϕ,c)f(\phi,c) by suitable cutoffs with parameter δ>0\delta>0 and then truncate the diffusion coefficients in the equation for the solute concentration cc with parameter ε>0\varepsilon>0. Because of the lack of a gradient estimate for cc, we add an artificial diffusion in the equation for cc (with parameter δ\delta). Finally, we solve the approximate system in a Faedo–Galerkin space with dimension N∈ℕN\in{\mathbb{N}}. Its global solvability follows from standard arguments and the energy inequality. After the limit N→∞N\to\infty, we are able to conclude the nonnegativity of the concentration. Then the entropy estimate and the artificial diffusion yield gradient bounds and we can pass to the limit ε→0\varepsilon\to 0. The most delicate part is the limit δ→0\delta\to 0 in the approximate system with solutions (ϕδ,cδ)(\phi_{\delta},c_{\delta}). The main idea is to derive a gradient bound for cδ3/2c_{\delta}^{3/2} and to apply the “nonlinear” Aubin–Lions lemma in the version of [5] to conclude the relative compactness of (cδ)(c_{\delta}) in L3​(Ω)L^{3}(\Omega). To identify the weak limit II, we proceed similarly as in [8, Section 3].

The paper is organized as follows. We derive the formal energy and entropy estimates in Section 2. The Faedo–Galerkin method and the limit N→∞N\to\infty are presented in Section 3. The limits ε→0\varepsilon\to 0 and then δ→0\delta\to 0 are performed in Sections 4 and 5, respectively.

2. Formal estimations

For the convenience of the reader, we derive the energy and entropy estimates formally for general energy densities f⁡(ϕ,c)f(\phi,c). Rigorous proofs on an approximate level are shown in Lemma 3.1 (energy inequality) and Lemma 4.2 (entropy inequality).

Proposition 2.1 (Energy equality).

Let (ϕ,c,μ)(\phi,c,\mu) be a smooth solution to (1.1)–(1.3) with the initial and boundary conditions (1.6)–(1.7), satisfying 0≤ϕ≤10\leq\phi\leq 1 in ΩT\Omega_{T}. Then

dd​tE(ϕ,c)+∫ΩM(ϕ)|∇μ−c∇∂cf(ϕ,c)|2dx+∫Ωce−ϕ|∇∂cf(ϕ,c)|2dx=0,\displaystyle\frac{d}{dt}E(\phi,c)+\int_{\Omega}M(\phi)|\nabla\mu-c\nabla\partial_{c}f(\phi,c)|^{2}dx+\int_{\Omega}ce^{-\phi}|\nabla\partial_{c}f(\phi,c)|^{2}dx=0,

recalling definition (1.8) of the energy E⁡(ϕ,c)E(\phi,c). If f⁡(ϕ,c)≥κ​c2f(\phi,c)\geq\kappa c^{2} holds for some κ>0\kappa>0, this gives a priori estimates for ϕ\phi in L∞​(0,T,H1​(Ω))L^{\infty}(0,T;H^{1}(\Omega)) and for cc in L∞​(0,T,L2​(Ω))L^{\infty}(0,T;L^{2}(\Omega)).

Proof.

We compute the time derivative, integrate by parts, and insert equations (1.1) and (1.2):

d​Ed​t\displaystyle\frac{dE}{dt} =∫Ω(−Δϕ∂tϕ+∂ϕf(ϕ,c)∂tϕ+∂cf(ϕ,c)∂tc)dx=∫Ω(μ∂tϕ+∂cf(ϕ,c)∂tc)dx\displaystyle=\int_{\Omega}\big(-\Delta\phi\partial_{t}\phi+\partial_{\phi}f(\phi,c)\partial_{t}\phi+\partial_{c}f(\phi,c)\partial_{t}c\big)dx=\int_{\Omega}\big(\mu\partial_{t}\phi+\partial_{c}f(\phi,c)\partial_{t}c\big)dx
=−∫Ω[M(ϕ)∇μ⋅(∇μ−c∂cf(ϕ,c))−cM(ϕ)∇∂cf(ϕ,c)⋅(∇μ−c∇∂cf(ϕ,c))\displaystyle=-\int_{\Omega}\big[M(\phi)\nabla\mu\cdot(\nabla\mu-c\partial_{c}f(\phi,c))-cM(\phi)\nabla\partial_{c}f(\phi,c)\cdot(\nabla\mu-c\nabla\partial_{c}f(\phi,c))
+ce−ϕ|∇∂cf(ϕ,c)|2]dx\displaystyle\phantom{xx}+ce^{-\phi}|\nabla\partial_{c}f(\phi,c)|^{2}\big]dx
=−∫ΩM(ϕ)|∇μ−c∇∂cf(ϕ,c)|2dx−∫Ωce−ϕ|∇∂cf(ϕ,c)|2dx,\displaystyle=-\int_{\Omega}M(\phi)|\nabla\mu-c\nabla\partial_{c}f(\phi,c)|^{2}dx-\int_{\Omega}ce^{-\phi}|\nabla\partial_{c}f(\phi,c)|^{2}dx,

which ends the proof. ∎

The second estimate involves the entropy density defined in (1.10).

Proposition 2.2 (Entropy equality).

Let (ϕ,c,μ)(\phi,c,\mu) be a smooth solution to (1.1)–(1.3) with the initial and boundary conditions (1.6)–(1.7), satisfying 0≤ϕ≤10\leq\phi\leq 1 in ΩT\Omega_{T}. The condition that ∂ϕ​c2f\partial_{\phi c}^{2}f is constant can be replaced by (i) ∂ϕ​c2f\partial_{\phi c}^{2}f does not depend on cc and is bounded, and (ii) c​∂ϕ​ϕ​c3f≤0c\partial_{\phi\phi c}^{3}f\leq 0. Indeed, by integrating by parts,

≤C​‖c‖L∞​(0,T,L2​(Ω))2​‖∂ϕ​c2f‖L∞​(ΩT)2+14​∫Ω(Δ​ϕ)2​𝑑x.\displaystyle\leq C\|c\|_{L^{\infty}(0,T;L^{2}(\Omega))}^{2}\|\partial_{\phi c}^{2}f\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega_{T})}^{2}+\frac{1}{4}\int_{\Omega}(\Delta\phi)^{2}dx.

In any case, we need that the potential ∂ϕf\partial_{\phi}f grows at most linearly in cc and that the energy ff contains a superlinear term in cc. Thus, we may generalize the nutrient part of the energy, but its structure needs to be similar to the function (ϕ,c)↦c2/2+c⁡(1−ϕ)(\phi,c)\mapsto c^{2}/2+c(1-\phi) considered in this paper.

3. Approximate solutions

We introduce first the approximate problem. To this end, we define for fixed δ>0\delta>0 the nondegenerate mobility

Mδ​(ϕ)={M⁡(δ)if ​ϕ≤δ,M⁡(ϕ)if ​δ≤ϕ≤1−δ,M⁡(1−δ)if ​ϕ≥1−δ.\displaystyle M_{\delta}(\phi)=\begin{cases}M(\delta)&\mbox{if }\phi\leq\delta,\\ M(\phi)&\mbox{if }\delta\leq\phi\leq 1-\delta,\\ M(1-\delta)&\mbox{if }\phi\geq 1-\delta.\end{cases}

The free energy density (1.5) is split into a convex part f1f_{1} and a nonconvex part f2f_{2}, where

f1​(ϕ)=ϕ​log⁡ϕ+(1−ϕ)​log⁡(1−ϕ),f2​(ϕ,c)=ϕ⁡(1−ϕ)+c22+c⁡(1−ϕ).f_{1}(\phi)=\phi\log\phi+(1-\phi)\log(1-\phi),\quad f_{2}(\phi,c)=\phi(1-\phi)+\frac{c^{2}}{2}+c(1-\phi).

We define an approximation of f1f_{1} on ℝ{\mathbb{R}} to remove the singularities at ϕ=0\phi=0 and ϕ=1\phi=1:

f1,δ​(ϕ)={f1​(δ)+f1′​(δ)​(ϕ−δ)+12​f1′′​(δ)​(ϕ−δ)2if ​ϕ≤δ,f1​(ϕ)if ​δ≤ϕ≤1−δ,f1​(1−δ)+f1′​(1−δ)​(ϕ−(1−δ))+12​f1′′​(1−δ)​(ϕ−(1−δ))2else,\displaystyle f_{1,\delta}(\phi)=\begin{cases}&f_{1}(\delta)+f_{1}^{\prime}(\delta)(\phi-\delta)+\frac{1}{2}f_{1}^{\prime\prime}(\delta)(\phi-\delta)^{2}\quad\mbox{if }\phi\leq\delta,\\ &f_{1}(\phi)\quad\mbox{if }\delta\leq\phi\leq 1-\delta,\\ &f_{1}(1-\delta)+f_{1}^{\prime}(1-\delta)(\phi-(1-\delta))+\frac{1}{2}f_{1}^{\prime\prime}(1-\delta)(\phi-(1-\delta))^{2}\quad\mbox{else},\end{cases}

and we set

Finally, we introduce the truncations

[ϕ]+1=min⁡{1,max⁡{0,ϕ}},[c]+ε=min⁡{1/ε,max⁡{0,c}},[\phi]_{+}^{1}=\min\{1,\max\{0,\phi\}\},\quad[c]_{+}^{\varepsilon}=\min\{1/\varepsilon,\max\{0,c\}\},

μ\displaystyle\mu =−Δ​ϕ+∂ϕfδ​(ϕ,c),\displaystyle=-\Delta\phi+\partial_{\phi}f_{\delta}(\phi,c),

with the initial and homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions

Observe that we added the artificial diffusion δ​Δ​c\delta\Delta c in (3.2) to obtain gradient bounds for cc. The truncations [c]+ε[c]_{+}^{\varepsilon} and [ϕ]+1[\phi]_{+}^{1} provide bounded diffusion coefficients needed to derive gradient bounds for the Faedo–Galerkin approximation. The existence of global weak solutions to the nondegenerate approximate problem (3.1)–(3.4) is shown in a classical way by means of the Faedo–Galerkin method, energy estimates, and a compactness argument. Since the estimations are strongly model-dependent, we present a full proof.

≤C∥cδ∇∂cf(ϕδ,cδ)∥L2​(ΩT)+C∥cδ∇ϕδ∥L2​(ΩT)≤C.\displaystyle\leq C\|\sqrt{c_{\delta}}\nabla\partial_{c}f(\phi_{\delta},c_{\delta})\|_{L^{2}(\Omega_{T})}+C\|\sqrt{c_{\delta}}\nabla\phi_{\delta}\|_{L^{2}(\Omega_{T})}\leq C.

achieving the second claim in (5.6). ∎

+‖e−[ϕδ]+1‖L∞​(ΩT)​‖cδ‖L4​(0,T,L8​d/(3​d−4)​(Ω))\displaystyle+\big\|e^{-[\phi_{\delta}]_{+}^{1}}\big\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega_{T})}\|\sqrt{c_{\delta}}\|_{L^{4}(0,T;L^{8d/(3d-4)}(\Omega))}

5.2. Compactness argument

The estimates obtained in the previous subsection allow us to complete the proof of Theorem 1.2.

Step 1: Convergence of (ϕδ)(\phi_{\delta})

We deduce from bound (5.7) that there exists a subsequence (not relabeled) such that, as δ→0\delta\to 0,

∂tϕδ⇀∂tϕ\displaystyle\partial_{t}\phi_{\delta}\rightharpoonup\partial_{t}\phi weakly in ​L2​(0,T,H1​(Ω)′).\displaystyle\quad\mbox{weakly in }L^{2}(0,T;H^{1}(\Omega)^{\prime}).

Taking into account estimate (5.5), we have, up to a subsequence,

(5.8) Δ​ϕδ⇀Δ​ϕweakly in ​L2​(ΩT).\displaystyle\Delta\phi_{\delta}\rightharpoonup\Delta\phi\quad\mbox{weakly in }L^{2}(\Omega_{T}).

Estimates (5.1), (5.5), (5.7), and the Aubin–Lions lemma show that

(5.9) ϕδ→ϕstrongly in ​L2​(0,T,H1​(Ω))∩C⁡([0,T],L2​(Ω)),\displaystyle\phi_{\delta}\rightarrow\phi\quad\mbox{strongly in }L^{2}(0,T;H^{1}(\Omega))\cap C([0,T];L^{2}(\Omega)),

which implies that ϕδ→ϕ\phi_{\delta}\rightarrow\phi a.e. in ΩT\Omega_{T}. Since exp⁡(−[ϕδ]+1)\exp(-[\phi_{\delta}]_{+}^{1}) is bounded in L∞​(Ω)L^{\infty}(\Omega), we have the convergence

e−[ϕδ]+1→e−[ϕ]+1strongly in ​Lp​(ΩT),p∈[1,∞).\displaystyle e^{-[\phi_{\delta}]_{+}^{1}}\rightarrow e^{-[\phi]_{+}^{1}}\quad\mbox{strongly in }L^{p}(\Omega_{T}),\quad p\in[1,\infty).

We need to verify that ϕ\phi lies between zero and one. Although the proof of the following lemma is very similar to [8], we present the full proof for the convenience of the reader.

Lemma 5.3 (Upper and lower bounds for ϕ\phi).

The limit function ϕ\phi satisfies 0<ϕ<10<\phi<1 a.e. in ΩT\Omega_{T}.

Proof.

twice to obtain

Φδ​(ϕδ​(t,x))=∫1/2ϕδ∫1/2sd​r​d​sδ2​(1−δ)2=(ϕδ−1/2)22​δ2​(1−δ)2.\displaystyle\Phi_{\delta}(\phi_{\delta}(t,x))=\int_{1/2}^{\phi_{\delta}}\int_{1/2}^{s}\frac{drds}{\delta^{2}(1-\delta)^{2}}=\frac{(\phi_{\delta}-1/2)^{2}}{2\delta^{2}(1-\delta)^{2}}.

In view of the a.e. convergence of (ϕδ)(\phi_{\delta}), this yields

meas⁡{(t,x):ϕ⁡(t,x)≥1+α}=limδ→0meas⁡(Vα,δ)≤limδ→02​C​δ2​(1−δ)2α2=0,\displaystyle{\rm meas}\{(t,x):\phi(t,x)\geq 1+\alpha\}=\lim_{\delta\rightarrow 0}{\rm meas}(V_{\alpha,\delta})\leq\lim_{\delta\rightarrow 0}\frac{2C\delta^{2}(1-\delta)^{2}}{\alpha^{2}}=0,

implying that ϕ⁡(t,x)≤1+α\phi(t,x)\leq 1+\alpha a.e. in ΩT\Omega_{T} for all α>0\alpha>0. Since α>0\alpha>0 is arbitrary, ϕ⁡(t,x)≤1\phi(t,x)\leq 1 a.e. in ΩT\Omega_{T}. In a similar way, we show that ϕ⁡(t,x)≥0\phi(t,x)\geq 0 a.e. in ΩT\Omega_{T}.

=−∫0T∫ΩM⁡(ϕ)c∇∂cf(ϕ,c)⋅Ψdxdt.\displaystyle=-\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\Omega}\sqrt{M(\phi)}c\nabla\partial_{c}f(\phi,c)\cdot\Psi dxdt.

Inserting the previous convergence results for I1I_{1}, I2I_{2}, and I3I_{3} into (5.15), we conclude that

∫0T∫ΩI⋅Ψ​𝑑x​𝑑t\displaystyle\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\Omega}I\cdot\Psi dxdt =∫0T∫Ω[Δϕdiv(M⁡(ϕ)Ψ)+(∇ϕ−2M⁡(ϕ)∇ϕ)⋅Ψ\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\Omega}\big[\Delta\phi{\rm{div}}\big(\sqrt{M(\phi)}\Psi\big)+\big(\nabla\phi-2\sqrt{M(\phi)}\nabla\phi\big)\cdot\Psi
+cdiv(M⁡(ϕ)Ψ)−M⁡(ϕ)c∇∂cf(ϕ,c)⋅Ψ]dxdt,\displaystyle\phantom{xx}+c\operatorname{div}\big(\sqrt{M(\phi)}\Psi\big)-\sqrt{M(\phi)}c\nabla\partial_{c}f(\phi,c)\cdot\Psi\big]dxdt,

finishing the proof of Theorem 1.2.
